title: How to Find the History of Your House
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a Leif Erikson Day joke and banter about their houses, then dig into how to research the history of a house, based on an article by Emily (Chuck's wife, a freelance writer for HowStuffWorks). Steps covered: talking to neighbors, the county recorder's office and deed history, plot numbers versus street addresses, Sanborn fire insurance maps, census, tax and occupation records, the Polk reverse city directory at the library, microfiche and newspaper clippings, library local history books, and reasons to research a house (architectural oddities, murders, ghosts, famous former owners, historic register listing, renovation). They also discuss East Lake in Atlanta and its history. The episode closes with listener mail about a fan who became a freelance writer, a Kiva lending team plug, and sign-off.

segments.title: Leif Erikson Day banter and house-age small talk
segments.summary: Hosts note it is Leif Erikson Day and recall a joke from a previous episode about the Norse. Josh and Chuck compare the ages of their houses and Josh describes a mysterious woven tarp in his yard. Josh introduces the topic, which Emily wrote about.

segments.title: Step one: talk to your neighbors
segments.summary: The first step in researching a house is asking neighbors. Chuck describes his new neighborhood and a former neighborhood where longtime residents knew local history, including a meth lab a few doors down.

segments.title: County recorder's office and deed history
segments.summary: Records are kept at the County Recorder's Office. Tracing the deed history back to the original owner can identify who built the home. Hosts note that old records are often on paper and not online, and that addresses change while plot numbers usually do not.

segments.title: Sanborn fire insurance maps
segments.summary: Sanborn maps were made for the fire insurance industry from 1867 onward and cover many US towns, plus some in Mexico, Canada, Cuba and whiskey distilleries. They show details such as windows, hydrants, building materials and street names and addresses.

segments.title: Census, tax records and the Polk directory
segments.summary: Census, tax assessor and survey records list names, ages and occupations of household members. The Polk reverse telephone directory at the library lets you search by address to find the occupant's name.

segments.title: Microfiche and newspaper research
segments.summary: If internet searches come up empty, microfiche at the library holds old newspapers that may have clippings about past owners, including murders. Josh and Chuck joke about the research process and about authors who write books after short research stints.

segments.title: Local history books and East Lake, Atlanta
segments.summary: Local history books may include pictures of houses. The hosts discuss Emily's research on East Lake in Atlanta, a turn-of-the-century farm turned lakeside suburb, and the Eastlake Country Club, which hosted a PGA tournament.

segments.title: Why research a house: architecture, murders, ghosts, famous owners
segments.summary: Reasons to research a house include architectural oddities, renovation to original condition, and curiosity about murders or ghosts. California and Hawaii require disclosure of ghostly activity when selling. A famous former owner could lead to historic register listing.

segments.title: Listener mail and Kiva plug
segments.summary: A listener who discovered the show while doing temp filing work wrote in after becoming a HowStuffWorks freelance writer. The hosts also plug the Stuff You Should Know Kiva lending team and invite listener stories.
